claims.evidence: This is based on serum analysis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The metabolic effects in Dicer knockouts were likely mediated at least in part by the loss of miR-122.
claims.source: At least in part, these effects were likely mediated by the loss of miR-122, whose inactivation has previously been shown to impact lipid metabolism (Krutzfeldt et al., 2005; Esau et al., 2006; Gatfield et al., 2009; Wen and Friedman, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on previous studies showing miR-122's role in lipid metabolism.

claims.claim: Nine miRNA seed families had more circadian targets than expected by chance specifically in the data set with higher mRNA/pre-mRNA ratios.
claims.source: Interestingly, this analysis revealed nine miRNA seed families with more circadian targets than expected by chance (Figure 6B) specifically in the data set with higher mRNA/pre-mRNA ratios.
claims.evidence: This is based on miRNA target prediction analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: miR-25, miR-92, miR-122, miR-22, and miR-29 are expressed at readily detectable levels in liver.
claims.source: Of these, miR-25, miR-92, miR-122, miR-22, and miR-29 are expressed at readily detectable levels in liver, as shown previously (Landgraf et al., 2007; Gatfield et al., 2009; Vollmers et al., 2009) and confirmed by northern blot (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and small RNA-seq (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data from the current study.

claims.claim: The reporter assay identified Per2 as the main miRNA-regulated core clock component in hepatocytes.
claims.source: Consistent with the RNA-seq and western blot analyses (Figure 3B,C), this assay indeed identified Per2 as the main miRNA-regulated core clock component (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is based on luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Per1 and Cry2 full-length 3′ UTRs showed 1.2-fold and 1.8-fold up-regulation, respectively, in Dicer knockout hepatocytes.
claims.source: Per1 and Cry2 full-length 3′ UTRs showed 1.2-fold and 1.8-fold up-regulation, respectively (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is based on luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The lack of strong Per1 regulation in liver was a striking difference to the MEF data.
claims.source: In particular, the lack of strong Per1 regulation in liver was a striking difference to the MEF data and could be responsible for phenotypic differences, as Chen et al. have proposed that the faster translation and higher accumulation of PERs (approximately twofold higher PER1 and PER2 peak levels in Dicer knockout) shortens the time delay within the oscillator's main feedback loop and speeds up the clock.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with the Chen et al. study.

claims.claim: miR-30 is among the most abundant miRNA species in liver (within the top 10 of miRNAs detected by small RNA-seq).
claims.source: It is possible that tissue-specific miRNA expression contributes to the observed differences; in line with a previous study (Vollmers et al., 2012), we have thus observed that miR-30 is among the most abundant miRNA species in liver (within the top 10 of miRNAs detected by small RNA-seq), but that miR-29 and miR-24 are expressed at lower levels (not in the top 50) (data not shown), which could thus partially explain the comparably weak effect of the Dicer knockout on PER1 in liver.
claims.evidence: This is based on small RNA-seq data and a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: miR-29 and miR-24 are expressed at lower levels in liver (not in the top 50 miRNAs detected by small RNA-seq).
claims.source: It is possible that tissue-specific miRNA expression contributes to the observed differences; in line with a previous study (Vollmers et al., 2012), we have thus observed that miR-30 is among the most abundant miRNA species in liver (within the top 10 of miRNAs detected by small RNA-seq), but that miR-29 and miR-24 are expressed at lower levels (not in the top 50) (data not shown), which could thus partially explain the comparably weak effect of the Dicer knockout on PER1 in liver.
claims.evidence: This is based on small RNA-seq data and a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The circadian system was globally very resilient to miRNA loss.
claims.source: Considering the severity of the genetic model, our finding that the circadian system was globally very resilient to miRNA loss was surprising and somewhat reminiscent of the stability of circadian oscillators with regard to other perturbations such as large fluctuations in general transcription rates and temperature (Dibner et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the overall findings of the study and a citation.

claims.claim: miRNAs frequently function in the fine-tuning and modulation of gene expression.
claims.source: Moreover, our findings are in line with the notion that miRNAs frequently function in the fine-tuning and modulation of gene expression (Krol et al., 2010; Fabian and Sonenberg, 2012; Yates et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to review articles.

claims.claim: Dicer knockout liver explants showed modest period lengthening of free-running rhythms (on average by 40 min).
claims.source: The hepatic core clock remained fully functional and showed only modest period lengthening of free-running rhythms (on average by 40 min) in Dicer knockout liver explants.
claims.evidence: This is based on bioluminescence analysis data from liver explants.

claims.claim: Mice in which Per2 levels are increased due to additional Per2 transgenes show period lengthening similar to Dicer knockout liver explants.
claims.source: This phenotype is a plausible consequence of the approximately twofold increase in expression of PER2, which we identified as the main miRNA-regulated core clock component in hepatocytes. Mice in which Per2 levels are increased due to additional Per2 transgenes thus show a similar period lengthening (Gu et al., 2012), while Per2 knockout mice have short periods before becoming arrhythmic (Zheng et al., 1999; Bae et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Per2 knockout mice have short periods before becoming arrhythmic.
claims.source: This phenotype is a plausible consequence of the approximately twofold increase in expression of PER2, which we identified as the main miRNA-regulated core clock component in hepatocytes. Mice in which Per2 levels are increased due to additional Per2 transgenes thus show a similar period lengthening (Gu et al., 2012), while Per2 knockout mice have short periods before becoming arrhythmic (Zheng et al., 1999; Bae et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The longer period seen in Dicer knockout liver explants is conceivably masked in the animal due to constant entrainment by the SCN and other cues.
claims.source: Conceivably, the longer period seen in Dicer knockout liver explants is masked in the animal due to constant entrainment by the SCN and other cues.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about why the phenotype is only observed in explants.

claims.claim: miRNAs confer robustness to oscillatory networks and denoise negative feedback loops.
claims.source: It is well possible that a phenotype will manifest in knockouts only under conditions that bring the steady-state relationship between entrainment cues and the liver clock out of equilibrium, such as in jet lag or food shifting experiments (Damiola et al., 2000); this situation would be consistent with models stating that miRNAs confer robustness to oscillatory networks and denoise negative feedback loops (Cohen et al., 2006; Gerard and Novak, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claims.claim: Per2 acts as a link between systemic entrainment signals and local liver clocks.
claims.source: Intriguingly, Per2 has already been noted to act as a link between systemic entrainment signals and local liver clocks (Kornmann et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Tissue-specific differences in miRNA activity likely form the basis of differences between liver and MEF Dicer knockout phenotypes.
claims.source: Interestingly, the previously reported dramatic period shorting (≈2 hr) in Dicer knockout MEFs (Chen et al., 2013) is in stark contrast to what we observed in liver. Very likely, tissue-specific differences in miRNA activity form the basis of these differences and could explain that PER1 and PER2 are equally strongly affected in Dicer knockout MEFs, whereas in liver PER1 appears to be less strongly regulated.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the current study with the Chen et al. study.

claims.claim: miR-219 and miR-132 are brain-specific regulators of period length and light-induced clock resetting, respectively.
claims.source: Interestingly, an earlier study on the SCN clock has revealed brain-specific miR-219 and miR-132 as regulators of period length and light-induced clock resetting, respectively (Cheng et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: miRNAs generally function to post-transcriptionally tune the core clock in a cell type-specific fashion.
claims.source: It is thus tempting to speculate that miRNAs generally function to post-transcriptionally tune the core clock in a cell type-specific fashion.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the tissue-specific differences observed.

claims.claim: miRNA activity could underlie known tissue-specific differences in phases and free-running period lengths.
claims.source: At least in part, miRNA activity could thus also underlie known tissue-specific differences in phases and free-running period lengths (Yoo et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Less than 2% of all rhythmic mRNAs fulfilled criteria for miRNA-driven rhythmicity.
claims.source: To this end, we found that miRNAs contributed only marginally to generating transcript rhythms at the post-transcriptional level. Less than 2% of all rhythmic mRNAs thus fulfilled our criteria for miRNA-driven rhythmicity and the identified examples (e.g., Figure 4E–I) showed low amplitude cycling.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: miRNAs are usually highly stable molecules and generally not expected to show pronounced daily variations in abundance.
claims.source: This finding is consistent with the notion that miRNAs are usually highly stable molecules and generally not expected to show pronounced daily variations in abundance (see below).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about miRNA stability.

claims.claim: For about 30% of the rhythmic transcriptome, miRNA-mediated regulation adds an additional layer of post-transcriptional control.
claims.source: By contrast, we have found that miRNAs exert important functions in refining the rhythmic mRNA accumulation profiles of cyclically transcribed genes. We thus estimate that for about 30% of the rhythmic transcriptome, miRNA-mediated regulation adds an additional layer of post-transcriptional control.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of rhythmic transcripts with increased mRNA/pre-mRNA ratios.

claims.claim: The absence of miRNAs caused a global shift of mRNA accumulation to later phases during the day.
claims.source: Concretely, the absence of miRNAs caused a global shift of mRNA accumulation to later phases during the day.
claims.evidence: This is based on phase analysis of RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Peak-to-trough amplitudes of mRNA accumulation were overall reduced in Dicer knockouts, although this effect was globally smaller and more variable across the transcriptome.
claims.source: Moreover, peak-to-trough amplitudes of mRNA accumulation were overall reduced in Dicer knockouts, although this effect was globally smaller and more variable across the transcriptome.
claims.evidence: This is based on amplitude analysis of RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: miRNAs are key to converting rhythmic transcriptional information into the desired tissue-specific rhythmic outcome.
claims.source: These results establish that miRNAs are in charge of an important regulatory control level sandwiched between rhythmic transcription and the final rhythmic mRNA and, eventually, protein output. Because many miRNAs are expressed in a tissue-specific fashion, they may thus be key to converting rhythmic transcriptional information into the desired tissue-specific rhythmic outcome.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the findings and knowledge of tissue-specific miRNA expression.

claims.claim: A discrete group of miRNAs (miR-25/92, miR-122, miR-22 and miR-29) is specifically involved in the post-transcriptional tuning of circadian transcripts in the liver.
claims.source: Our miRNA target prediction analysis would suggest that a discrete group of miRNAs (miR-25/92, miR-122, miR-22 and miR-29) is specifically involved in the post-transcriptional tuning of circadian transcripts in the liver.
claims.evidence: This is based on miRNA target prediction analysis.

claims.claim: Several miRNAs have been previously reported as potentially rhythmic in mouse liver.
claims.source: Several miRNAs have been previously reported as potentially rhythmic in mouse liver (Na et al., 2009; Vollmers et al., 2012), but our small RNA-seq profiling (data not shown), as well as previous analyses of individual miRNAs (Gatfield et al., 2009) could not confirm high-cycling miRNA species.
claims.evidence: This is based on small RNA-seq data and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The recently reported circadian expression of Dicer itself was not evident from the RNA-seq data.
claims.source: Similarly, the recently reported circadian expression of Dicer itself (Yan et al., 2013) was not evident from our data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and a citation.

claims.claim: The potential for rhythmic miRNA activity in mouse liver is relatively low.
claims.source: Collectively, these findings suggest that the potential for rhythmic miRNA activity in mouse liver is relatively low.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of evidence for rhythmic miRNAs.

claims.claim: In a few exceptional cases, miRNA biogenesis can be independent of canonical Dicer processing, for example for miR-451.
claims.source: First, in a few exceptional cases, miRNA biogenesis can be independent of canonical Dicer processing, for example for miR-451 (Yang and Lai, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: miR-451 is not depleted from Dicer knockout livers.
claims.source: This miRNA is indeed not depleted from Dicer knockout livers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is based on microarray data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Genome-wide measurements of miRNA action on mRNA and protein levels have shown that these correlate generally well.
claims.source: This approach seems justified overall because genome-wide measurements of miRNA action on mRNA and protein levels have shown that these correlate generally well (Baek et al., 2008; Selbach et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: miRNAs may affect mRNA levels less strongly than protein levels.
claims.source: Nevertheless, it should be kept in mind that miRNAs may affect mRNA levels less strongly than protein levels (Selbach et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2010), and that mRNA changes can even be absent altogether (e.g., Bhattacharyya et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: miRNAs have been reported to directly interfere with transcription through promoter complementarity.
claims.source: However, in specific cases miRNAs have been reported to directly interfere with transcription through promoter complementarity (reviewed in Huang and Li, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

results.result: A conditional Dicer knockout mouse model was successfully established in hepatocytes, achieving efficient miRNA depletion approximately 1 month after tamoxifen treatment, with miR-122 levels reduced to 1.4% of control levels and pre-miR-122 accumulating to >6-fold higher levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C31 collectively demonstrate successful establishment of the Dicer knockout model with appropriate validation. The PCR, northern blot, and microarray data (C26-C28, C31) provide converging evidence for efficient knockout. The observation of miRNA recovery after 2 months (C29-C30) is appropriately interpreted as hepatocyte renewal from escaped cells.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis using a strategy that quantifies both mRNAs and pre-mRNAs revealed that 30.3% of mRNAs and 15.5% of pre-mRNAs were significantly changed in Dicer knockouts, with changes skewed toward increased mRNA levels and a global shift in mRNA/pre-mRNA ratios to higher values.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C43 describe the RNA-seq methodology and results with appropriate statistical analysis. The use of pre-mRNA abundance as a proxy for transcription rates is well-supported by citation (C37-C38), and the differential expression analysis with 1.5-fold cutoff is clearly documented with percentages and directionality (C40-C43).

results.result: Increased mRNA/pre-mRNA ratios in Dicer knockouts are predictive of miRNA activity, as validated by the observation that miR-122 targets showed increased ratios while miR-124 targets (negative control) and ribosomal protein mRNAs did not.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45 provide appropriate positive and negative controls for validating the mRNA/pre-mRNA ratio as a metric for miRNA regulation. The use of experimentally validated targets for liver-expressed miR-122 versus non-expressed miR-124, along with ribosomal proteins with short 3' UTRs, represents sound experimental design.

results.result: Per1, Per2, and Per3 showed moderate but significant increases in mRNA/pre-mRNA ratios in Dicer knockouts, with PER2 protein levels increased ~2-fold and CRY2 increased 1.5-fold, while PER1 protein was barely increased (1.1-fold), yet core clock functionality remained overall unimpaired.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C51, C54-C55 demonstrate effects on core clock components with converging evidence from RNA-seq and western blot. The discrepancy between Per1 mRNA and protein levels (C50) is acknowledged but not fully explained. The conclusion that the core clock remains functional (C51, C55) is supported by unchanged expression of clock-regulated genes like Dbp.

results.result: Dicer knockout liver explants showed a trend toward period lengthening with periods on average 41 minutes longer than controls, but this effect did not reach statistical significance (p=0.197).
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 report a phenotype that fails to reach statistical significance. While the 41-minute difference is biologically interesting and consistent with increased PER2 levels, the lack of statistical significance (p=0.197) means this result cannot be considered definitively supported. The sample sizes (n=9 control, n=13 knockout) may be insufficient to detect this effect.

results.result: Rhythmicity analysis revealed that approximately 13-14% of mRNAs and 17% of pre-mRNAs were rhythmic in both control and Dicer knockout mice, with >60% of oscillating mRNAs also rhythmic at the pre-mRNA level, and Dicer KO-specific rhythmic transcripts enriched for cell cycle genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 describe comprehensive rhythmicity detection with appropriate methodology combining JTK_CYCLE and harmonic regression. The percentages are consistent with previous literature (cited in C56-C57). The enrichment of cell cycle genes in KO-specific rhythmic transcripts (C60) is supported by GO term analysis and consistent with liver regeneration after miRNA loss.

results.result: While 30% of rhythmic transcripts in control mice showed significantly increased mRNA/pre-mRNA ratios in Dicer knockouts, visual inspection identified no more than 20 transcripts (~2% of rhythmic mRNAs) with confident miRNA-driven rhythmicity, indicating miRNAs are only of marginal importance as drivers of circadian rhythmicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C64, C96 provide converging evidence that miRNAs rarely drive rhythmicity de novo. The analysis combines quantitative metrics (C61-C62) with careful visual inspection (C63), and the conclusion (C64, C96) is appropriately conservative. The low percentage (<2%) is consistent with the expectation that miRNAs are generally stable molecules.

results.result: Loss of miRNAs caused rhythmic mRNAs with increased mRNA/pre-mRNA ratios to peak on average 48 minutes later than controls (p=1.72e-07) and showed globally shallower amplitudes with a mean 7% decrease, with phase delays being the dominant, consistent consequence and both effects individually highly significant by permutation testing.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C68, C73-C74 demonstrate effects of miRNA loss on rhythmic gene expression with appropriate statistical analysis. The phase delay effect is highly significant (C67) and validated by permutation tests (C74). The amplitude effect is smaller and more variable (C68) but still significant. The kinetic model framework (C65) provides theoretical support for the observations.

results.result: For Lipa, rhythmicity generated at the pre-mRNA level was completely lost at the mRNA level when miRNAs were absent, and since LAL has been reported to be rhythmic in liver but non-rhythmic in other organs, miRNAs could be involved in rendering Lipa rhythms tissue-specific.
results.evaluation: Claim C69 is supported by RNA-seq data showing loss of Lipa mRNA rhythmicity in Dicer knockouts. However, claim C71 is speculative about tissue-specific roles of miRNAs. While the hypothesis is plausible given the cited tissue-specific rhythmicity of LAL (C70), direct evidence for miRNA involvement in tissue-specificity is lacking.

results.result: Serum analyses of Dicer knockout animals showed reduced cholesterol, triglyceride, and glucose levels, effects likely mediated at least in part by loss of miR-122.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 report metabolic phenotypes with appropriate measurements. The attribution to miR-122 loss (C76) is reasonable given extensive prior literature on miR-122's role in lipid metabolism (cited), though the contribution of other miRNAs cannot be excluded in this global knockout model.

results.result: miRNA target prediction analysis identified nine miRNA seed families with more circadian targets than expected by chance in transcripts with higher mRNA/pre-mRNA ratios, with miR-25, miR-92, miR-122, miR-22, and miR-29 expressed at readily detectable levels in liver and specifically involved in post-transcriptional tuning of circadian transcripts.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78, C102 describe enrichment analysis with appropriate statistical methods. The identification of specific miRNA families is supported by both computational prediction and expression validation by northern blot and small RNA-seq (C78). The conclusion about their involvement in circadian regulation (C102) is appropriately framed as a suggestion based on the enrichment analysis.

results.result: Luciferase reporter assays in primary hepatocytes identified Per2 as the main miRNA-regulated core clock component with full-length 3' UTR showing strong de-repression, while Per1 showed only 1.2-fold up-regulation, a striking difference from MEF data potentially explained by tissue-specific miRNA expression patterns with miR-30 highly abundant but miR-29 and miR-24 expressed at lower levels in liver.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 provide functional validation of miRNA regulation using an appropriate reporter system. The differential regulation of Per2 vs Per1 (C79-C80) is consistent with the protein data. The comparison to MEFs (C81) and proposed explanation based on tissue-specific miRNA expression (C82-C83) is reasonable, though the small RNA-seq data supporting miRNA abundance claims is not shown.

results.result: The hepatic core clock was surprisingly resilient to miRNA loss, yet whole transcriptome sequencing uncovered widespread effects on clock output gene expression, with cyclic transcription paired with miRNA-mediated regulation affecting up to 30% of the rhythmic transcriptome and serving to post-transcriptionally adjust phases and amplitudes of rhythmic mRNA accumulation, establishing miRNAs as key to converting rhythmic transcriptional information into tissue-specific rhythmic outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C6, C8, C84, C98-C101 represent the major conclusions of the study, supported by the comprehensive RNA-seq analysis and functional studies. The resilience of the core clock (C3, C84) is demonstrated by maintained rhythmicity of core clock genes. The widespread effects on output genes (C4) and the 30% estimate (C5, C98) are supported by the mRNA/pre-mRNA ratio analysis. The phase and amplitude adjustments (C6, C99-C100) are statistically validated. The conclusion about tissue-specificity (C8, C101) is a reasonable inference.

results.result: Dicer knockout liver explants showed modest period lengthening of free-running rhythms (on average by 40 min), a phenotype consistent with increased PER2 levels and similar to mice with additional Per2 transgenes, potentially masked in vivo by constant SCN entrainment and consistent with models of miRNAs conferring robustness to oscillatory networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C91 attempt to interpret the non-significant period lengthening result. While the biological reasoning is sound and supported by citations (C87-C88, C90-C91), the core observation (C86) lacks statistical significance (see C52-C53). The speculation about masking by SCN entrainment (C89) is plausible but untested. This interpretation requires additional experimental validation.

results.result: Tissue-specific differences in miRNA activity likely form the basis of differences between liver and MEF Dicer knockout phenotypes, suggesting miRNAs generally function to post-transcriptionally tune the core clock in a cell type-specific fashion and could underlie known tissue-specific differences in phases and free-running period lengths.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 propose tissue-specific miRNA functions based on comparison with MEF data (C92) and SCN data (C93). While the hypothesis is plausible and supported by the differential regulation of Per1 between tissues, claims C94-C95 are explicitly speculative. Direct evidence for tissue-specific miRNA tuning of the clock would require comparative studies across multiple tissues.

results.result: Small RNA-seq profiling could not confirm high-cycling miRNA species previously reported in mouse liver, and circadian expression of Dicer itself was not evident from RNA-seq data, suggesting the potential for rhythmic miRNA activity in mouse liver is relatively low.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 report negative findings regarding rhythmic miRNAs with appropriate acknowledgment of conflicting prior reports (C103-C104). The conclusion about low potential for rhythmic miRNA activity (C105) is a reasonable inference from the data, though the authors appropriately note this approach cannot definitively resolve the issue of rhythmic miRNA activity.

results.result: miR-451, which can undergo Dicer-independent biogenesis, is not depleted from Dicer knockout livers.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 identify an important limitation of the Dicer knockout approach. The Dicer-independent processing of miR-451 is established knowledge (C106), and its persistence in knockouts is confirmed by microarray data (C107). This represents appropriate acknowledgment of model limitations.

results.result: While genome-wide measurements show miRNA action on mRNA and protein levels generally correlate well, miRNAs may affect mRNA levels less strongly than protein levels, and in specific cases miRNAs can directly interfere with transcription through promoter complementarity.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 appropriately discuss limitations of using mRNA levels as a proxy for miRNA activity. All claims are supported by citations to prior literature. This represents appropriate acknowledgment of methodological limitations and alternative mechanisms of miRNA action.
